extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Deseret News interested in books, authors, and literary ethics
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion column evaluating allegations of plagiarism by a nonfiction historian/author, describing evidence, past incidents, and professional consequences. It argues whether those allegations should affect how readers and institutions treat the author's current lectures and books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary definition of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Webster's dictionary says that plagiarism is 'to steal and pass off as one's own the ideas or words of another — or 'to commit literary theft.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard meaning: taking others' words or ideas and presenting them as your own is plagiarism. This frames subsequent judgments about specific passages as potential 'literary theft.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent/number of borrowed passages
rubrics_metrics.description: The most serious instances, at least 40 borrowed passages, were found to be in her 900 page book, 'The Kennedys and the Fitzgeralds' (1987).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude matters: dozens of borrowed passages across a long work suggest extensive problems rather than isolated mistakes. Count and proportion of lifted text are relevant to assessing seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim copying / exact phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many examples showed that the words and phrases used by Goodwin were often exact copies of those used by McTaggart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim matches (exact wording or phrases) constitute strong evidence of plagiarism compared with loose paraphrase; side-by-side identical language is a key indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to attribute / improper use of quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodwin's argument when confronted was to blame it on her 'careless' habit of 'taking notes in longhand.' She told The New York Times, 'If I am writing up a passage ... and part of it is from other people's writing, I just type it up and put it in a footnote.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not using quotation marks for verbatim text and relying on footnotes (or failing to attribute clearly) is inadequate. Proper inline quotation and explicit attribution are required to avoid plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern / repeated offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomas Mallon alleges that those who commit plagiarism 'almost always do it more than once.' Goodwin's tendency to steal the words of others was actually discovered 15 years earlier when Lynne McTaggart found massive copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A history of prior incidents increases culpability; a one-time mistake differs from a repeating pattern. Recurrence suggests deliberate or systemic problems rather than isolated carelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement or payment as indicia of wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted, she agreed to pay McTaggart an undisclosed sum of 'hush money' so that the incident would not be made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private settlements or payments to resolve plagiarism claims may be taken as evidence that the accused recognized wrongdoing or that the copying was substantial, though settlements are not formal admissions in every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability when using researchers/assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: She worked with an assembly line of four researchers, and allegedly, when she looked at their notes and her own, she could not always distinguish between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation of research does not absolve the named author of responsibility for attribution. Authors should have systems to track sources so that borrowed text from assistants is correctly credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing side-by-side examples as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many examples of Goodwin's account as compared to McTaggart's were published in newspapers and magazines so that the reader could see that the words and phrases used by Goodwin were often exact copies of those used by McTaggart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing public, side-by-side comparisons of suspect passages is a persuasive method to demonstrate copying and allows independent evaluation of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional and institutional consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequently, universities around the country that had invited Goodwin to deliver commencement addresses disinvited her. She was dropped as a historical commentator on PBS's 'The Newshour with Jim Lehrer.' Publishers promised new editions of some of her books but never delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional actions (disinvitations, removal from roles, publishing decisions) reflect how organizations assess the severity of allegations and affect an author's professional standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission (or lack of admission) influences trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since she has never admitted to plagiarism in spite of overwhelming evidence against her, I think Goodwin's lectures and books should both be taken with a grain of salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an author admits error matters for readers' trust. Lack of admission in the face of evidence may justify continued skepticism toward current and future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of recent charges does not erase past concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Then the scandal just died down, and Goodwin kept writing; her latest is about Lincoln ... So far, no charges of plagiarism have been leveled at her latest book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of new accusations or formal charges for later works does not necessarily exonerate earlier misconduct; past documented problems remain relevant when evaluating present output.
